abstract: Gene genealogies along a chromosome are dependent not only because nearby alleles tend to experience no recombination and are therefore inherited together, but also because alleles at different loci may share parental histories through a common ancestor. Disentangling physical linkage and shared parental trajectories is key to understanding how demography shapes genetic diversity. We develop a mathematical framework for describing the joint genealogies of sampled alleles in a finite admixed population, tracing their ancestry backward to the source populations while explicitly accounting for parental relationships and recombination events. Under a Wright--Fisher model, we show that the joint gene genealogy forms an absorbing Markov chain, derive the likelihood of local ancestry, and connect it to other quantities of interest, notably the admixture fraction. We further establish that, once demographic parameters become constant, local ancestry converges to distinct limiting distributions depending on the demographic setting. Under isolation, chromosomes undergo infinitely many recombination events and linkage disequilibrium is due to drift within population replicates, retaining traces of past admixture events. Under constant gene flow from source populations, recent contributions progressively erase the influence of earlier ancestry. Using the joint genealogy of two alleles, we obtain the limiting variance of admixture fractions in both regimes. We illustrate our framework's flexibility through simulations of endogamy and selection. These examples show how genetic diversity depends on the structure of underlying parental relationships. Our work provides a framework for specifying and analyzing complex demographic scenarios and clarifies the links between local ancestry and mating patterns.
